strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: adapting pretrained MLLMs to video reasoning segmentation without task-specific training. Object–background subtraction and video–frame fusion form a simple, coherent approach.

The reported improvements are substantial. With Qwen2.5VL-7B, DecAF improves over Loc-Head from 64.0 to 75.2 J&F on Ref-DAVIS and from 41.6 to 59.7 on ReasonVOS. The latter nearly matches Veason-R1's 59.9 without additional training.

Evaluation spans five datasets, three model families, and multiple model sizes. Applying the proposed SAM2 prompting pipeline to Loc-Head also provides a useful controlled comparison of attention quality.

Ablations support the contributions of contrastive fusion, complementary fusion, higher-resolution frames, vision-aware rollout, and tracklet scoring. Full prompt templates and qualitative failure cases provide useful additional transparency.
weaknesses: Baseline validation remains unresolved. Appendix C reports reproducing Loc-Head at 34.4 versus its published 74.2 on RefCOCO, an unusually large discrepancy requiring investigation. TAM is evaluated under the proposed object-focused prompt despite acknowledged incompatibility. LLaVA comparisons additionally use different checkpoints. Comparisons with VL-SAM and a competitive language-guided grounding-plus-SAM2 pipeline are missing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the exact weighted rollout aggregation and residual normalization are underspecified, as are Gaussian smoothing parameters, actual input resolutions and tiling settings, evaluation splits, and several propagation details. The text alternates between extracting attention from the final query token and from generated responses. No usable code link is supplied.

The attention consistency score has a structural bias against multiple or briefly visible targets: each tracklet is normalized by attention mass across the entire video and all objects. Under unit-bounded attention and SAM confidence scores, the default tracklet threshold requires an attention consistency score of at least 0.4 even when the other two scores are maximal. This can reject correct individual objects when attention is distributed across several targets. Object-count and visibility-stratified evaluation is needed to substantiate the multi-object claim.

Inference cost is unmeasured despite multiple video/frame object and background passes, an additional category-selection query, attention rollout, and potentially many SAM2 hypotheses. Runtime, peak memory, candidate counts, and scaling with video length are important to assess the practical value of this training-free pipeline.

Novelty is primarily an empirical combination of established attention rollout, contrastive subtraction, multiscale fusion, and proposal filtering. The paper does not isolate whether background-specific semantics outperform generic prompt subtraction or whether video–frame fusion outperforms a compute-matched ensemble.

Claims of comparability to trained methods need qualification: DecAF trails Veason-R1 by 11.0 J&F on ReVOS overall and 13.1 on its reasoning subset, and trails VRS-HQ by 13.4 on Ref-YTVOS. These substantial gaps receive limited analysis.

There are evaluation-reporting concerns. Table 2 lists Loc-Head/InternVL3 ReasonVOS scores of J=47.0 and F=43.3 but J&F=39.6, which is arithmetically inconsistent. Hyperparameter ablations include the test-only ReasonVOS benchmark without explaining a separate selection protocol.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: adapting pretrained MLLMs to video reasoning segmentation without additional training. Background subtraction, video–frame fusion, and attention-guided SAM2 tracklet selection form a coherent pipeline.
Evaluation spans five datasets and three MLLM families. With Qwen2.5VL-7B, DecAF improves over the reported Loc-Head baseline from 64.0 to 75.2 J&F on Ref-DAVIS and from 41.6 to 59.7 on ReasonVOS.

The component ablations provide concrete supporting evidence. Tables 4–7 examine contrastive fusion, video–frame fusion, resolution, rollout weighting, thresholds, and tracklet scoring, with substantial gains attributable to multiple components.
The appendix provides prompt templates and candid failure examples, including incorrect rejection of large objects and briefly visible targets.
weaknesses: Baseline reliability remains a significant concern. Appendix C reports reproducing Loc-Head at 34.4 versus its published 74.2 on RefCOCO validation, without resolving this discrepancy. Applying the same SAM2 pipeline helps control downstream processing but does not establish that the baseline attention extraction is correct. TAM is evaluated under the authors’ object-focused prompt despite acknowledged incompatibility, and the LLaVA comparison uses different checkpoints.

The contribution is primarily an empirical combination of existing attention rollout and SAM prompting with subtraction, averaging, and heuristic scoring. The ablations establish usefulness, but comparisons against simpler negative prompts, alternative tracklet scoring, and an end-to-end VL-SAM adaptation would better establish the distinct contribution.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The weighted rollout lacks an explicit equation specifying aggregation normalization and residual handling; Gaussian smoothing parameters and exact input resolutions are omitted. Dataset splits and the development protocol for choosing thresholds and other design decisions are insufficiently specified. ReasonVOS is described as test-only yet used extensively for ablations, so independence from test-set-driven design needs clarification.

Inference cost is unreported despite repeated object/background MLLM passes over video and individual high-resolution frames, attention rollout, and multiple SAM2 tracklets. Runtime, peak memory, candidate counts, and comparisons under matched inference budgets are needed to assess practical value.

Claims of comparability to trained methods require qualification. The strongest configuration is competitive on Ref-DAVIS and ReasonVOS, but trails Veason-R1 by 11.0 J&F on ReVOS overall and VRS-HQ by 13.4 on Ref-YTVOS. The evaluation also lacks quantitative breakdowns for object absence, multiple objects, and temporal reasoning that would substantiate the proposed mechanisms.

Table 2 contains a substantive reporting inconsistency: Loc-Head with InternVL3 on ReasonVOS lists J=47.0 and F=43.3 but J&F=39.6, which cannot be their mean. This should be corrected before interpreting that comparison.

The reported gains are substantial. With Qwen2.5VL-7B, DecAF improves over Loc-Head from 64.0 to 75.2 J&F on Ref-DAVIS, 41.6 to 59.7 on ReasonVOS, and 43.8 to 50.3 on ReVOS.

Evaluation spans five datasets and three model families, with additional model-size experiments. Applying the proposed SAM2 prompting to Loc-Head provides a useful comparison of the underlying localization signals.

The ablations provide concrete support for the components. Background subtraction, video–frame fusion, multiscale processing, vision-aware head weighting, and tracklet scoring each improve performance. Shared prompt templates and disclosed failure cases are also positive.
weaknesses: Baseline reliability remains unresolved. Appendix C reports reproducing Loc-Head at 34.4 versus its published 74.2 on RefCOCO validation. Replacing its downstream prompting helps the comparison but does not establish that the remaining implementation is faithful. TAM is evaluated under the proposed object-focused prompt despite acknowledged incompatibility, and the LLaVA comparison uses different checkpoints. These issues weaken the broad superiority claim.

The contribution is primarily an empirical combination of established attention rollout, contrastive subtraction, multiscale fusion, and segmentation proposal filtering. The ablations establish usefulness, but the conceptual advance over prior attention-based grounding remains modest.

Inference cost is entirely unreported. Multiple video and high-resolution frame passes, attention extraction and rollout, and potentially numerous SAM2 proposals could be expensive. Runtime, peak memory, proposal counts, and scaling with video length are needed to assess practical value.

Important reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous: exact input resolutions and tiling settings, Gaussian smoothing parameters, the complete weighted aggregation/residual normalization formula, and the precise decoding token used for attention extraction. The manuscript also does not clearly identify a held-out protocol for choosing thresholds and rollout settings; ReasonVOS is described as test-only but used extensively in ablations.

Claims of comparability with trained methods need qualification. Results are strong on ReasonVOS and Ref-DAVIS, but DecAF trails Veason-R1 by 11.0 J&F on ReVOS and 8.7 on MeViS, and trails VRS-HQ by 13.4 on Ref-YTVOS.

The global denominator in the attention-consistency score can disadvantage small or briefly visible objects and individual tracklets in multi-object scenes. The appendix acknowledges related failures, but provides no quantitative breakdown. Table 2 also contains an inconsistent Loc-Head/InternVL3 ReasonVOS entry: J=47.0 and F=43.3 cannot average to the reported 39.6.

strengths: The paper presents an effective training-free approach to video reasoning segmentation. Object–background contrast, video–frame fusion, and attention-guided SAM2 tracklet selection form a coherent pipeline with practical value.

The empirical gains are substantial. With Qwen2.5VL-7B, DecAF improves over Loc-Head from 64.6 to 75.2 J&F on Ref-DAVIS and from 41.1 to 63.9 on ReasonVOS. Appendix E also compares against native Qwen grounding with SAM2, including a matched 16-frame configuration, which reaches only 64.8 and 48.0.

Evaluation covers five datasets, three MLLM families, and multiple model sizes. The ReasonVOS result exceeds the reported trained competitors, providing concrete evidence that the approach is competitive beyond a narrow proof of concept.

Extensive ablations support the individual components, including contrastive fusion, temporal–spatial fusion, higher-resolution frame inputs, vision-aware head weighting, and tracklet scoring. The appendix adds prompt sensitivity experiments, similar-object evaluation, and informative failure cases.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is primarily an empirical combination of established attention rollout, contrastive subtraction, multiscale fusion, and SAM prompting. The evidence supports this combination's effectiveness more strongly than the broader claim that reasoning capability directly translates into localization; there is no controlled analysis isolating reasoning from improved spatial grounding.

Inference efficiency is unreported. Multiple video/frame object and background passes, explicit attention extraction and rollout, and potentially many SAM2 mask proposals could be expensive. Runtime, peak memory, candidate counts, and scaling with video length and resolution are needed to assess the practical tradeoff of avoiding training.

Baseline reliability remains partly unresolved. Appendix C reports reproducing Loc-Head at 34.4 versus its published 74.2 on RefCOCO validation. Adapting its sink heuristics and giving it the proposed SAM pipeline are constructive measures, but this large discrepancy warrants further verification. TAM is evaluated under prompting acknowledged to be poorly suited to it, without a stronger token-aggregation adaptation.

Important implementation and evaluation details remain ambiguous: the exact weighted aggregation and residual normalization for V-Max, Gaussian smoothing parameters, model-specific input resolutions, and how the attention-dependent tracklet scoring is applied to native-grounding baselines. The protocol for selecting thresholds and rollout layers should also be stated, particularly because substantial ablation work uses the test-only ReasonVOS benchmark.

Attention consistency scoring has a structural limitation: Equation 8 normalizes each tracklet by foreground attention mass across the entire video, which can penalize small, briefly visible, or individual objects within multi-object targets. The appendix acknowledges related failures, but does not quantify them by visibility duration or object count. Performance is also not uniformly comparable to leading trained methods: DecAF remains behind on ReVOS and Ref-YouTube-VOS.

strengths: DecAF provides a useful training-free video segmentation pipeline combining contrastive attention, video–frame fusion, and attention-guided SAM2 selection. Its contribution is supported by substantial empirical improvements.
Evaluation spans five datasets and three MLLM families. With Qwen2.5VL-7B, DecAF achieves 63.9 J&F on ReasonVOS versus 41.1 for Loc-Head and 59.9 for the strongest reported trained comparator.

The ablations meaningfully support individual components. On Ref-DAVIS, background subtraction improves performance from 61.9 to 75.2, while video–frame fusion outperforms either modality alone. Rollout normalization and tracklet scoring also provide measurable gains.

The appendix strengthens the evaluation with native Qwen grounding baselines, prompt variations, similar-object analysis, and explicit failure cases. Applying the proposed SAM2 pipeline to competing grounding methods helps isolate attention quality.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily an empirical combination of existing attention rollout, subtraction, multiscale fusion, and SAM prompting. The paper provides limited analysis explaining when these mechanisms should succeed beyond the tested settings.

Baseline reproduction remains a concern: Appendix C reports reproducing Loc-Head at 34.4 versus its published 74.2 on RefCOCO validation. Adapting the SAM pipeline helps, but this discrepancy warrants resolution before attributing all observed weaknesses to the competing method. TAM is also evaluated under a prompting setup acknowledged to be poorly suited to it.

No inference latency, peak memory, or compute comparison is reported despite multiple video/frame passes, high-resolution processing, attention extraction, and mask propagation. Avoiding training does not establish practical computational efficiency.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the weighted rollout aggregation and residual normalization are not fully specified, and exact input resolutions, Gaussian smoothing parameters, and decoding settings are missing. The protocol for selecting hyperparameters independently of the evaluation sets is also unclear.

Equation 8 normalizes each tracklet against attention mass across the entire video, potentially penalizing correct small or briefly visible targets and individual instances in multi-target queries. The appendix acknowledges related failures, but performance is not systematically characterized by target count, size, or visibility duration.

Claims of competitiveness with trained methods need qualification: DecAF trails the strongest reported results on ReVOS, MeViS, and Ref-YouTube-VOS. Benchmark improvements also do not by themselves establish the stronger conclusion that reasoning capability directly translates into localization.

strengths: DecAF offers a useful training-free approach to video reasoning segmentation, combining object–background attention subtraction, video–frame fusion, and attention-guided SAM2 tracklet selection.

The quantitative gains are substantial. With Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DecAF improves over Loc-Head from 64.6 to 75.2 J&F on Ref-DAVIS and from 41.1 to 63.9 on ReasonVOS. The latter also exceeds the reported trained baselines.
Evaluation covers five datasets, three MLLM families, and multiple model sizes. Appendix E strengthens the comparisons by evaluating native Qwen2.5-VL grounding with the same SAM2 pipeline.

Extensive ablations support the main components. Background subtraction, complementary fusion, vision-aware rollout, and attention consistency scoring each provide measurable benefits. Prompt variations and qualitative failure cases are also examined.
weaknesses: Baseline reliability remains a concern. Appendix C reports reproducing Loc-Head at 34.4 versus its published 74.2 on RefCOCO validation without resolving this discrepancy. Sharing the improved SAM2 pipeline helps comparison fairness, but does not establish that the underlying baseline is faithfully reproduced. TAM is also evaluated with a prompt acknowledged to be poorly suited to it.

The computational tradeoff is unmeasured. Multiple object/background passes over video and high-resolution frames, attention rollout, and candidate-mask propagation could be expensive. No latency, peak memory, hardware, or compute-matched comparison is provided.

Several implementation details remain underspecified, including the precise weighted-head aggregation and residual normalization, Gaussian smoothing parameters, input-resolution budgets, and backward propagation for tracklets initialized after the first frame. These omissions limit reproducibility.

Equation 8 normalizes each tracklet against attention mass across the entire video, potentially penalizing correct small, brief, or individual targets in multi-target scenes. The appendix acknowledges related failures, but the similar-object subset mainly tests distractor discrimination rather than performance as the number of jointly referred targets increases.

The novelty is primarily an effective integration of existing attention and segmentation mechanisms. Claims about directly translating reasoning into localization exceed the mechanistic evidence, and competitiveness with trained methods is uneven: DecAF trails the strongest reported results on ReVOS and Ref-YouTube-VOS.
